title: Operational Harmony: Sprint Architectural Guide for Cross-Functional SLO Adoption
content:
Purpose

This working guide outlines a pragmatic, architecture-focused sprint cadence to onboard product and infra services into the Reliability Program (SLO-first approach). It aims to align engineering, product, SRE, and platform teams around a repeatable sprint pattern that delivers measurable SLO adoption, telemetry baseline, runbooks, and rollback/runway controls — with minimal disruption to feature velocity.

Context & Problem Statement

We have many partial efforts: feature teams with ad-hoc alerts, platform owners with metrics but no shared SLO taxonomy, and product teams without clear customer impact mapping. The program needs a lightweight but prescriptive pattern so teams can adopt SLOs without reinventing instrumentation or operational workflows each time.

High-level goals (quarter view)
- Define a minimal SLO adoption template that can be completed in 3 sprints per service.
- Instrument key signals (latency p95/p99, error-rate, user-visible failure rate) with traceable owners.
- Deliver runbooks and an ops-oncall playbook for each adopted service.
- Run two canary rollouts using the new canary gating + SLO guardrails.
- Surface unit economics (cost/sec and p99 latency) and show one cost optimization experiment per service.

Scope and Out of Scope\- Scope:
- Public API endpoints, model-serving frontends, background batch jobs with direct customer-facing impact.
- Integration with existing observability stack (Prometheus/OpenTelemetry/Tempo/Grafana).
- Template runbooks and canary gates implemented as code (playbooks + automation scripts).

- Out of scope:
- Deep refactor of model-serving architecture (heavy infra rewrites), full org-wide enforcement, or legacy monoliths requiring >3 months work.

SLO adoption template (minimal)
1) Define user journeys and SLOs (1 week)
   - Owner(s): product + service lead
   - Output: 1–2 user-facing SLOs with target (e.g., 99.9% success rate over 30d; 95th/99th latency limits).
   - Example: "chat-generation API: successful completion within 600ms for 99% of requests over 30d"

2) Instrument signals & baselining (1 sprint)
   - Owner(s): infra/observability + service engineers
   - Tasks: add tracing spans, HTTP/GRPC metrics, user-visible error tagging, export histograms for latency buckets, ensure high-cardinality keys avoided in base metrics
   - Output: baseline dashboard and auditable metric definitions (metric name, type, owner).

3) Runbook + Alert tuning + Canary (1 sprint)
   - Owner(s): SRE + service lead
   - Tasks: author runbook, define alert thresholds derived from SLO/SLI (not raw), implement canary rollout automation and guarded rollback policy, train on-call with tabletop exercise.
   - Output: service runbook, canary gating config, post-deployment checklist.

Cross-functional roles and responsibilities
- Product Owner: define user journeys, prioritize which endpoints map to SLOs.
- Service Lead / Tech Lead: implement instrumentation and own the SLO target.
- Observability Engineer: support metric creation, maintain dashboards and ensure signal quality.
- SRE: author runbooks, define oncall playbooks, set canary criteria and rollback actions.
- Platform/Serving Runtime: ensure runtime-level metrics (kv-cache hit rate, batch latency) are exported and explainable.
- Data/Telemetry Owner: ensure retention, cardinality guardrails, and sampling policy.

Sprint blueprint (3-sprint example for a single service)
Sprint 0 (planning, kickoff) — week 0
- Kickoff with stakeholders (30–60 min). Confirm service boundary, user journeys, and expected SLIs. Create Jira epic (JIRA-OPS-xxxx).
- Acceptance: SLO definition agreed and documented.

Sprint 1 (instrument & baseline) — weeks 1–2
- Add metrics and tracing hooks, validate metric types, create dashboard with baseline windows (7d, 30d).
- Acceptance: Baseline dashboard shows >= 14d of valid data or simulated traffic to emulate baseline.

Sprint 2 (runbook + canary + alerts) — weeks 3–4
- Implement runbook, alert-to-SLO mapping, and canary automation. Run tabletop with SRE.
- Acceptance: Canary passes under simulated noise and SLO guardrails; runbook reviewed and ready.

Operational gating & Canary policy (template)
- Canary length: 30–60 minutes for latency-sensitive endpoints, 1–4 hours for lower-risk releases.
- Canary pass criteria: no increase >2x baseline error-rate and p99 latency within tolerated delta for canary/users.
- Automated rollback triggers: sustained error rate above SLO-derived threshold for >5m or p99 latency spike beyond rollback delta for >3m.

Instrumentation checklist
- Avoid using high-cardinality labels in base metrics (use static tags in logs instead).
- Add OpenTelemetry span names for key model-serving actions: tokenize -> encode -> kv_cache_hit -> infer -> decode.
- Export error classification: user_error | model_error | infra_error.
- Capture request metadata needed for debugging (request_id, route_id, model_version) but do not expose PII.

Observability & dashboards
- Core dashboard panels: SLO health (burn rate), latency histogram, error taxonomy pie, throughput/units, traces-per-error example.
- Add an "ops checklist" widget showing last runbook review date, last canary date, and open postmortem count.

Quality gates and acceptance criteria (for the adoption epic)
- SLO defined and approved by product and SRE.
- SLIs instrumented with >= 95% of traffic accounted for (no signal holes).
- Dashboards show >= 14d of consistent telemetry or synthetic load validation.
- Runbook has a clear page in the runbook repo and a trained oncall in last-30-day tabletop.
- Canary automation exists and has been executed in a non-prod environment.

Runbooks & postmortem policy
- Minimal runbook sections: symptoms, quick triage steps, mitigation actions, escalation path, rollback steps, owners.
- Postmortem: any SLO breach of >= 6h or customer-impacting incident triggers a postmortem with a clear remedial plan and timeline.

Integration checkpoints (handoff matrix)
- Week 0: product -> service lead SLO signoff.
- Week 1: observability confirms metric types and dashboard layout.
- Week 2: SRE reviews runbook draft.
- Week 3: Platform validates runtime-level metrics are present.
- Week 4: Canary execution and signoff.

Risk register (top items)
- Signal quality gaps: missing spans or sampled traces. Mitigation: synthetic traffic and telemetry QA process.
- Alert fatigue: thresholds too low. Mitigation: use burn-rate derived alerts, reduce noisy alerts and move to paging only for severe breaches.
- Regression risk during instrumentation: add feature flags and staged rollout for metric changes.

Experimentation & optimization ideas (per-service)
- Small batching profile experiment: measure cost/token vs p99 latency and pick Pareto-optimal point.
- KV cache TTL tuning: track cache-hit delta vs model latency and set safe default.
- Quantization sanity check: run inference on a canary subset and compare output-quality regressions with automated evals.

Communication plan
- Weekly reliability standup (30m) with cross-functional reps to review adoption progress (blocked services, telemetry issues, canary results).
- Slack channel: #ops-slo-adoption for asynchronous questions + quick triage.
- Monthly stakeholder digest: concise summary of SLO coverage, incidents, and cost/latency experiments.

Deliverables and success metrics (quarterly)
- % of eligible services with at least one active user-facing SLO (target 60% by quarter end).
- Mean time to detect (MTTD) for SLO degradations (target: reduce by 30%).
- Number of successful canary rollouts with gating automation (target: 4).
- Cost-per-1k-requests delta for services that ran optimization experiments.

Open questions / Decisions needed
- Enforcement: will adoption be advisory or required for new services? (Decision owner: Head of SRE)
- Metric retention policy: default retention for SLO metrics vs long-term analytics (Decision owner: Observability team)
- Canonical SLO window lengths (30d vs 7d short-window for release cadence).

Next steps (this week)
- Triage three candidate services for the initial pilot (Priya to propose list by 2026-02-16).
- Create Jira epics for each pilot; add acceptance criteria checklist.
- Observability team to publish the minimal metric template and sample dashboards.

Notes from kickoff (2026-02-12)
- Quick decisions: prefer 30d SLO window by default, but allow 7d short-window for rapid releases.
- Agreed to log SLO decisions in Confluence and reference Jira epics by tag.

Action items
- Aisha: draft pilot selection criteria and share with product leads (due 2026-02-16).
- Diego: prepare synthetic load harness to generate baseline traffic (due 2026-02-20).
- Priya: publish minimal metric naming convention and example dashboards (due 2026-02-19).
- Marcus: create canary automation template and a checklist for rollback triggers (due 2026-02-22).

Appendix: Example minimal SLO templates
- Availability SLO (simple):
  name: "api_success_rate"
  target: "99.9% over 30d"
  SLI: "ratio of requests with status = 200 or 2xx and model_response.success = true"
  owner: "service-lead"

- Latency SLO (histogram-based):
  name: "api_p95_latency"
  target: "p95 <= 600ms over 30d"
  SLI: "p95 from request_duration_seconds histogram computed over 30d rolling window"
  owner: "service-lead"
